summary.text: If \(2n\) is not a sum of two primes, every matrix entry is zero, since the two numbers tested at position \((i,j)\), \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\), sum to \(2n\); hence the determinant vanishes. For \(k\ge 60\), taking \(n=2k+1>120\) contradicts the assumed nonvanishing unless \(4k+2=2n\) has a two-prime decomposition, while the finitely many cases \(0<k<60\) are handled by explicit prime pairs.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)=A228623(n)\). Thus, for each positive integer \(n\), let \(M_n\) be the \(n\times n\) matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by \(i,j\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\), and whose \((i,j)\)-entry is
\[
 (M_n)_{ij}=\begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Then \(a(n)=\det(M_n)\). (The displayed quantities are positive: for example, \(n+i-j\ge n-(n-1)=1\), and similarly \(n+j-i\ge1\). Thus there is no ambiguity from subtraction in the natural numbers.)

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement
\[
  n>120\text{ and }n\text{ odd}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(n)\ne0.
\]
We prove that for every integer \(k>0\), the integer \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

We first record the determinant observation on which the argument rests.

**Lemma.** If \(n>0\) and \(2n\) is not a sum of two primes, then \(a(n)=0\).

**Proof of the lemma.** Consider any indices \(i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). Because \(j<n\), we have \(j\le n+i\), and because \(i<n\), we have \(i\le n+j\). Consequently the two subtractions in
\[
 p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i
\]
are ordinary exact subtractions, and
\[
 p+q=(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n.
\]
If the \((i,j)\)-entry of \(M_n\) were \(1\), then by definition both \(p\) and \(q\) would be prime. They would therefore give a representation \(2n=p+q\) as a sum of two primes, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence every entry of \(M_n\) is zero, so \(M_n\) is the zero matrix. Since \(n>0\), this matrix has at least one row (indeed, all its rows are zero), and its determinant is \(0\). Therefore \(a(n)=0\), proving the lemma. \(\square\)

We now fix \(k>0\). There are two cases.

### Case 1: \(k<60\)

Here \(k\) is one of \(1,2,\ldots,59\). The following table gives, for every such \(k\), primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(p+q=4k+2\):

\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
k&(p,q)& &k&(p,q)&\\ \hline
1&(3,3)&&21&(3,83)&&41&(3,163)\\
2&(3,7)&&22&(7,83)&&42&(3,167)\\
3&(3,11)&&23&(5,89)&&43&(7,167)\\
4&(5,13)&&24&(19,79)&&44&(5,173)\\
5&(3,19)&&25&(5,97)&&45&(3,179)\\
6&(3,23)&&26&(3,103)&&46&(5,181)\\
7&(7,23)&&27&(3,107)&&47&(11,179)\\
8&(3,31)&&28&(5,109)&&48&(3,191)\\
9&(7,31)&&29&(5,113)&&49&(5,193)\\
10&(5,37)&&30&(13,109)&&50&(3,199)\\
11&(3,43)&&31&(13,113)&&51&(7,199)\\
12&(3,47)&&32&(3,127)&&52&(11,199)\\
13&(7,47)&&33&(3,131)&&53&(3,211)\\
14&(5,53)&&34&(7,131)&&54&(7,211)\\
15&(3,59)&&35&(3,139)&&55&(11,211)\\
16&(5,61)&&36&(7,139)&&56&(3,223)\\
17&(3,67)&&37&(11,139)&&57&(3,227)\\
18&(3,71)&&38&(3,151)&&58&(5,229)\\
19&(5,73)&&39&(7,151)&&59&(5,233)\\
20&(3,79)&&40&(5,157)&&&
\end{array}
\]

For each row, direct addition gives \(p+q=4k+2\). All the displayed numbers are prime. This can be checked by trial division: every displayed number is at most \(233\), so for each one it is enough to check that it is divisible by none of the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) that do not exceed its square root (with only those divisors at most the particular number's square root needing to be tested). Thus the required Goldbach representation exists for every \(1\le k<60\).

### Case 2: \(k\ge60\)

Set
\[
 n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd. Moreover,
\[
 n=2k+1\ge2\cdot60+1=121>120.
\]
The assumed nonvanishing conjecture therefore gives
\[
 a(n)\ne0.
\]
We claim that \(4k+2\) must be a sum of two primes. Suppose, for contradiction, that there are no primes \(p,q\) with
\[
 4k+2=p+q.
\]
But
\[
 2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2,
\]
so this supposition says exactly that \(2n\) is not a sum of two primes. Since \(n>0\), the lemma then yields \(a(n)=0\), contradicting \(a(n)\ne0\). Hence primes \(p,q\) with \(4k+2=p+q\) do exist.

The two cases cover every positive integer \(k\). Therefore, under the assumption that \(a(n)\ne0\) for every odd \(n>120\), every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is a sum of two primes.
